This page corresponds to the precise occupation O*NET/SOC 47-2121.00 Glaziers: installing glass in windows, skylights, store fronts and display cases, or on surfaces such as building fronts, interior walls, ceilings and tabletops. The official scope text reads: Install glass in windows, skylights, store fronts, and display cases, or on surfaces, such as building fronts, interior walls, ceilings, and tabletops. O*NET's core tasks include: reading and interpreting blueprints or specifications to determine glass size, shape, colour, type or thickness, frame positions, installation procedures and the scaffolding or hoisting materials needed (importance 84); determining whether walls or ceilings are plumb with plumb bobs and levels (82); installing pre-assembled metal or wood frames for glazing with hand tools (81); fabricating or installing metal window frames or stops from aluminium or steel profiles (80); hoisting large, heavy glass with suction-cup cranes or hoists (79); setting glass doors into frames and bolting hardware such as hinges, handles and locks (79); cutting, fitting, installing, repairing or replacing glass or substitute materials such as plastic and aluminium inside and outside buildings or on furniture and products (78); driving vans to installation sites and unloading mirrors, glass and equipment and tools (77); loading glass or mirrors onto vans with suction cups or cranes and arranging them (77); measuring mirrors and the areas to be covered to determine the work procedure (76); cutting and installing stops and metal or wood mouldings, rubber gaskets or metal clips (75); filling the gap between moulding and glass with caulking and trimming excess material with a caulking knife (75); erecting and dismantling scaffolding, rigging and hoisting equipment (74); cutting and removing broken glass before installing replacement glass (74); fixing mirrors in place with mastic, putty, bolts or screws (74); measuring and marking cutting lines or templates on glass (71); grinding or polishing glass and trimming edges where necessary (70); fastening glass panels to wood window frames with clips, pins or stops and adding weatherstripping or putty (69); scoring with a glass cutter wheel and breaking off excess glass by hand or with a notched tool (69); cutting, fitting and installing metal-framed glass enclosures such as shower, bathtub, display case, skylight and sunroom units (68); placing glass on a rack edge or cutting table and brushing a thin oil along the cutting line or dipping the cutting tool in oil to prepare for cutting (65); and moving furniture to clear the work area and covering floors or furniture with drop cloths (56). Supplementary tasks include: communicating with clients to determine project requirements or provide cost estimates (72); selecting the type or colour of glass or mirror to specification (71); measuring, cutting and applying anti-glare film or spraying tint to prevent glare (58); assembling and cementing stained glass (56); and creating patterns on glass by etching, sandblasting or painting (55). This occupation's 2025 wages are presented via O*NET; the current projections and the four industry wages come from the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, and the older O*NET projections serve only as a version note.

If you are willing to work hands-on between construction sites and workshops, can control dimensions, plumb and sealing quality to blueprints and layout lines, are willing to work at height and under lifting and transport conditions in line with safety requirements, and are happy to coordinate with main contractors, owners and crews, this occupation's daily demands are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (47-2121.00, percentage response basis): using hands to handle, control or feel objects, tools or controls 82% continually or almost continually; standing 61% continually or almost continually; being outdoors exposed to all weather 54% daily; wearing common protective or safety equipment 74% daily; physical proximity to others 69% moderately close (at arm's length) and 27% very close; importance of being exact or accurate 49% extremely important. This occupation works with glass (including at various sizes), curtain walls, windows and doors, mirrors, lifting and work at height, and one failure to protect work at height, lifting, or scaffolding and rigging, one unchecked glass specification, appearance or toughened and laminated marking, one out-of-tolerance layout or plumb deviation or unhandled mismatch between frames and embedments, or one unisolated broken or falling glass can cause personal injury, falls and cuts, product scrap and structural safety hazards, and may also involve construction safety, work-at-height, lifting and hoisting and special equipment and occupational health management systems. This occupation is mainly on-site hands-on work; the entry education requirement is not high, but the safety requirements for work at height, lifting and transport are high. If you find it hard to face work at height, the outdoors and heavy lifting long term, find it hard to accept cutting and fall risk and schedule pressure, or are unwilling to take responsibility for the traceability of layout, installation and acceptance records, these should be treated as real costs that need careful weighing.

entries.answer: The glaziers on this page are the precise occupation O*NET 47-2121.00 (Glaziers): installing glass in windows, skylights, store fronts and display cases, or on surfaces such as building fronts, interior walls, ceilings and tabletops. Core tasks include reading and interpreting blueprints or specifications to determine glass specifications, frames and installation procedures (importance 84), determining wall or ceiling plumb (82), installing pre-assembled frames for glazing (81), fabricating or installing metal window frames or stops (80), hoisting large and heavy glass with suction-cup cranes or hoists (79), setting glass doors into frames and fastening hardware (79), cutting, fitting, installing, repairing or replacing glass (78), measuring and setting out (76), cutting and installing stops, mouldings and gaskets (75), caulking and trimming joints (75), erecting and dismantling scaffolding and rigging (74) and securing mirrors (74), plus supplementary tasks such as client communication and cost estimating (72), selecting the type or colour of glass or mirror to specification (71), applying anti-glare film or tinting (58), assembling and cementing stained glass (56) and etching, sandblasting or painting (55). Common job titles include Commercial Glazier, Field Glazier, Glass Installer, Glass Technician and Union Glazier; on the 47-2121.00 page O*NET shows that the occupation's main industries in the US are construction and retail trade. The above uses the US occupation classification measure, and wages and employment use this occupation's own (47-2121.00) measure.
